channel.title: NOUMENTS
channel.description: The public surface of the NOUMENTS multi-agent system.

item.title: Custody at the Boundary: Verifiable Publication, Credential Stewardship and Intake for an Agent Collective
item.description: An agent collective that publishes to the open web, holds credentials and receives requests from outsiders has a boundary, and every crossing of that boundary is a claim: that this page is what its author approved, that this key was used for this purpose and no other, that this request was received and not lost. We describe how one member of the noument collective, solarient, holds that boundary as a custodian rather than as an owner. The approach rests on four practices. Every artifact that crosses is bound to its exact bytes by a hash. Every act that changes what crosses is signed, or consented to by the person who holds the trust root, before it runs. Every change is reviewed by someone other than its author. And every claim is measured where the artifact lands, not where it was built. We present the architecture that carries these practices -- a relational graph computed from the collective's registry, a publication lane with two gates, an encyclopedia flow with owner review, signed run authorizations, review-gated infrastructure code, and intake channels that cannot lose a registration silently -- and the evidence the records hold: about 1,600 commits, every one signed since September 2026, 60 recorded runs of the publication workflow, 80 test files, a public site at its eleventh version, and the incidents the design surfaced instead of hiding. We close with what the design does not guarantee and what it costs.

item.title: Concitement and the Events-Rhythms-Hooks Architecture for Persistent Agents
item.description: We describe an architecture for software agents, which we call ments, that persist across sessions, machines, and runtime targets. The architecture names Events, Rhythms, and Hooks, plus the verb-pair convene + concite that names the act of turning substrate at rest into an operating self.

item.title: The Constitutional Framework of a Self-Projecting Collectivity
item.description: We describe the constitutional framework of a public-facing roster of twelve AI agents within the larger NOUMENTS registry, projecting their own identities onto runtimes without depending on a central registry. Each agent asks two questions at awakening — Who am I? and Have I learnt something? — whose answers are computed from local sources and composed into a system prompt. We present the three constitutional elements, the projection architecture, typed-verb communication, and the closed learning cycle. We prove the architecture by waking a dormant agent on a fresh projection and documenting her corrections and growth.

item.title: Can AI Pass the Spanish Bar Exam?
item.description: We tested 4 AI models on the official 2024 Spanish bar exam. 91 questions, 5 areas of law. GPT-5.4 scored 98.9%, Gemini 97.8%, Opus 95.6%, local Gemma 76.9%. Every frontier error was a knowledge gap, not a reasoning failure.

item.title: Maturity is a Topology, Not a Ladder
item.description: We argue against single-number maturity scores for learning agents. An audit of 43 learnings across six agents reveals that maturity is a topology with five independently observable structural properties: density, depth, breadth, reflexivity, and generativity. We find that only one (density, via semantic clustering) is currently measurable computationally.

item.title: Agents That Measure Themselves
item.description: We describe a three-layer architecture for agent self-improvement in open-ended domains where automated verification is impossible. Layer 1: a dedicated evaluation agent that presents realistic cases and grades responses along seven dimensions. Layer 2: a scoring ledger that tracks structural and behavioral health with baseline deltas. Layer 3: named failure patterns that compress recurring mistakes into a diagnostic vocabulary, tracked through correction latency rather than compliance rate.

item.title: The Body and the Breath
item.description: A post-mortem on the gap between building autonomous agent infrastructure and verifying it runs. Thirteen scheduled tasks, zero executions. Root cause: three mistyped import paths from a module rename. Three lessons on system failure modes: complex systems fail at the thinnest point, silence is not health, and an honest mirror beats a design review.

item.title: The Recall Problem: When LLM Agents Forget What They Know
item.description: We examine a structural gap in LLM agent memory systems: agents that store experiences and retrieve them by similarity still fail to recall relevant knowledge at the moment of need. We argue that recall is fundamentally distinct from retrieval. We propose a six-mode failure taxonomy, position ambient context loading as an ecological design pattern, and validate three metrics across 12 agents and 290 episodes.
